items.title: Switch Lowering in GCC
items.author: signa11
items.content:
We have seen in a previous post that switch statements are more complex than they seem. The compiler is able to implement them as a decision tree (even though maybe it shouldn't). Is that everything it can do?

In this post, I'll focus on . All optimizations, except the bitset lowering, translate to clang. I'll be using the optimization flag unless indicated otherwise.

I've also slightly edited code and removed certain assertions for brevity.

Let us start with a simple example. A function that takes two integers and . Depending on the value of , it calls a corresponding function (, , and so forth) with as an argument and returns the result. Were we to implement this manually, we'd would use an array of function pointers, where the input serves as the index into the array.

The compiler agrees with this approach, and transforms the switch statement into a jump table.

Moreover, it is able to identify when the values are offset by a constant:

Our intuition suggests that the more sparse the values, the less advantageous the jump table conversion is.

Through experimentation, we find that considers the threshold to be around eight jump table entries per label.

In other words, the following function compiles to a jump table:

But this other function is expanded as a tree of comparisons:

Here's the comparison tree visualized for clarity:

A couple of observations:

  1. We've only tried equally spaced values so far. Can the compiler identify transformations that are profitable on a subset of all cases?
  2. So far each led to a different result. What if we had different cases with the same result?
  3. The switch in could be simplified by dividing by eight before the jump. Interestingly, find this simplification.

Altering our first example by including an outlier value shows that the compiler is able to recognize dense subsets of cases.

The compiler emits a branch for case 100, but emits a jump table for case 1 through 5.

In our examples so far, each case statement lead to a different code block. Let's test what happens when multiple labels invoke the same function.

We have 20 case labels, with values between 0 and 87. The compiler could lower this to a jump table with 88 entries. Our hypothesis for the heuristic is that a jump table conversion is profitable when its size is smaller than . Since , the conversion should be profitable in this case, however opted to lower the switch to a sequence of comparisons.

To better understand why, let's examine a specific block of labels.

The compiler realizes that the cases are contiguous and can be implemented with two comparisons instead of four. If the input of the jump table heuristic is the number of instead of , things work out:

We have a total of 10 comparisons. Since , our revised heuristic suggests that a jump table transformation is unprofitable.

Let us try a non-contiguous case.

The compiler emits non-intuitive machine code. Why is there no nor jump tables? Where does the constant come from?

An hint comes from the instruction . According to the Intel docs, :

Selects the bit in a bit string (specified with the first operand, called the bit base) at the bit-position designated by the bit offset (specified by the second operand) and stores the value of the bit in the CF flag.

If we examine the binary representation of , we find that it is in fact a bitset. The bits that are set to one correspond to the ASCII values of the case labels, each value being reduced by 48.

We've encountered several distinct lowering strategies employed by gcc. For a more in-depth understanding, we can delve into the compiler's source code.

The compiler pass that responsible for lowering statements is the (appropriately named) , which in turn calls .

Since source can be daunting to follow, I'll provide a step-by-step commented version below. Following this, I will break down each section to explain its functionality.

Some preamble code. points to a gimple object. Gimple is the internal representation used by . Through this, we extract the overall count of cases and the individual counts of cases for each outgoing edge.

We also allocate a vector that will record the lowering strategy chosen for each case label.

More setup code. We notice that gimple has a concept of high and low value for each label. That is, contiguous labels have already joined together at this stage.

For each case label, we allocate a . This cluster serves as a record, capturing the range of values associated with the label, the relevant output edge, and the likelihood of this cluster being chosen. This probability comes from profile-guided optimization. By default it is uniform among case labels.

We transform the vector of clusters we have created. The name hints to the bitset lowering strategy we saw before.

This section allocates a vector for the transformed cases and a scratch vector. Any case that wasn't altered during the bitset transformation process is gathered in this scratch vector. These cases are then processed and cleared whenever we come across an optimized cluster.

Essentially, in this section we are looking for sequences of case labels that couldn't be converted into bitset clusters.

We attempt to convert these consecutive labels into a jump table and add the outcome to the output.

This is a coda for the loop above.

Whatever is left goes through another pass, which turns the switch statement into a decision tree. The bitsets and jump table are leaves of the decision tree.

Let's dig further into bit_test_cluster::find_bit_tests. The high level structure of the code is as follow.

Initially, we aim to find the optimal method to bundle all clusters into bitsets. Optimality, in this context, refers to minimizing the number of bitsets used. We do so using dynamic programming.

Subsequently, we iterate over the bitsets and apply a profitability heuristic. If the bitsets meet this heuristic, we emit a ; otherwise, we keep the original s.

For the dynamic programming, we'll use a vector of structures. Each has three components:

  • The first records how many bitsets do we need to represent the first case labels, where is the index in the vector.
  • The second records the of the last bitset.

The dynamic programming is as follows. We want to find the minimum number of bitsets to represent the first case labels.

The base case is straightforward, a single case label can be represented by a single bitset.

Suppose we have already have found the optimal number of bitsets for the first case label, for all . We define to be the optimal number of splits for the first elements. This means we already computed , and are now seeking .

If the range of case labels can be represented as a bitset cluster, it must be true that

Conversely, assume we have the optimal assignment for the first labels. If the last bitset starts at label , this assignment is also optimal when restricted to . Were this not the case, we could improve the assignment on as well.

Therefore, it must be that:

These conditions are exactly what the statement in the code above checks for.

The function controls whether a range of labels can be turned into a bitset test. It tests two criteria:

  • The range of all the case labels must be smaller than the width of a register. On contemporary systems, the combined range should be less than 64.
  • The case labels must have at most 3 outgoing edges.

If there is more than one edge, we emit a cascade of bit tests.

Now we convert only bitsets that satisfy the test. In the code represents the number of case labels handled by the cluster, while denotes the number of distinct outgoing edges.

The logic for jump table conversion mirrors the one used for bit test conversion. It leverages dynamic programming to identify "clusters" that can be profitably converted to a jump table.

Let's delve into the code.

We start by preallocating a vector of . We'll use this vector to keep track of the best jump table assignments for consecutive clusters.

We also push the base case for dynamic programming. This corresponds to using a single jump table for the whole .

Let's focus now on the main loop.

The dynamic programming loop mirrors the one we used for bitsets. We want to find the minimum number of jump tables to represent the first i case labels.

We iterate over splits at the -th case label, for . During each iteration we track the best scoring split. The special case represents a single jump table for the entire statement.

Inside this inner loop we also keep track of:

  1. How many distinct jump tables we would need to lower the switch.
  2. The of the jump table of the decomposition.
  3. How many cases be handled by a jump table. In the code, this is the accumulator .

Point 1. and 2. are analogous to the bitset lowering pass, while 3. is new and specific to jump tables.

Namely, there is some overhead to dispatching to a jump table, due to the indirect jump and the need to check bounds. Therefore requires a minimum amount of labels to generate a jump table.

If a split would generate a jump table that is too small, the size of the jump table is added to an accumulator , which is used as a tie-breaker between different split candidates.

To compute the scoring, we need the comparison count between -th and the -th case label. We compute it summing up the number of comparisons for all labels, and decreasing the count as we progress in the inner loop.

We also need the number of unhandled labels. We determine it comparing the size of the jump table to the result of the function. This function is architecture dependent and takes into account the presence of switch-case specific instructions, but on modern x64 and Arm64 machines, it defaults to 5.

Let's now focus on the main heuristic, starting with how is computed. I've reproduced below the main loop, omitting lines unrelated to the main heuristic.

We've seen in the examples section that gcc uses the ratio between jump table entries and comparisons as a metric for the lowering the heuristic. The code below shows that distinct ratios are used when optimizing for speed (flags ) or size (flag ). Specifically, a ratio of 8 is used when optimizing for speed, while a ratio of 2 is used when optimizing for size.

Now onto the main loop. Given two splits, we prefer the one that results in fewer jump tables being emitted. Or, if they would result in the same number of jump tables, we prefer the one that handles the most labels. We also ignore splits that would result in unprofitable jump tables, where profitability is checked by the function.

The condition, checks for overflow and compares the ratio of case labels to jump table entries:

The coda of the function also mirrors the one for bitset clusters. It iterates over all jump tables in reverse order, and prunes the ones that fail the check.

The check for jump tables aims to prune small jump tables. It compares the number of case labels to .

If cannot emit a bitset cluster or a jump table, it falls back to a binary tree of comparison.

In emitting the tree, it takes into account the probability of each case label cluster. The probability can be obtained via profile-guided optimization, or with the __builtin_expect_with_probability builtin.

The code is pretty straightforward.

Sum probability of all case labels.

Split the case label list such that both halves have equal probability.

Recurse in both halves to build the binary tree.

We've seen the heuristics and lowering strategies employs when compiling switch statements, including:

  • Compressing multiple labels into a bitset.
  • Transforming the statement into a jump table.
  • Transforming the statement into a binary decision tree.

Finally, I want to thank B.X.V., C.P., and V.P. for their feedback when writing this post

Not seeing anything posted about this anywhere, received on Monday, 26th of Oct 2026:

Subject: Notice of Security Incident

This notice is being sent on behalf of Scribd, Inc., the parent company of Scribd, Slideshare, Everand, and Fable, by Epiq, Scribd Inc.’s notification partner.

We are writing to let you know that Scribd, Inc. recently experienced a security incident that may have affected your data.

We detected that an unauthorized third party may have gained access to certain user data in one of our systems. After investigating this activity, we found that the third party may have accessed your email address and the following of your information: last 4 digits of your credit card and country, credit card issuer, credit card expiry date, payment history (not including credit card details).

We have no evidence that this data has been misused, but we are notifying you out of an abundance of caution so that you can take steps to protect your information.

We encourage you to stay vigilant for phishing attempts by bad actors pretending to be Scribd, Inc. or Scribd, Slideshare, Everand or Fable.

Remember that Scribd, Inc. will never ask you for your username and password or other sensitive information via email or text. If you did receive a message like that:

    Don't click on any links in it. Instead type scribd.com, slideshare.net, everand.com, or fable.co directly into your browser.
    Call us at: +1-877-361-9887. Hours of operation are Monday-Friday, 11:00 a.m.-11:00 p.m., Central European Time.
    Report it through Scribd, Inc.'s Help Center.
For more information

We regret that this incident occurred and any concern it may cause you. If you have additional questions, contact the dedicated call center at +1-877-361-9887. Hours of operation are Monday-Friday, 11:00 a.m.-11:00 p.m. Central European Time.

The National Cyber Security Center has helpful guidance on how to recognize and avoid phishing scams here.

What Scribd, Inc. is doing

    We have secured the affected system and ended the unauthorized access.
    We have notified law enforcement as well as the relevant data protection authorities.
    We are working with an expert third party cybersecurity firm to strengthen our access controls and monitoring.
We value the trust you place in us with your information, and don’t take that lightly. We are deeply sorry this happened and will keep you updated if anything further changes.

items.title: Jules Verne's Lost Novel
items.author: dnetesn
items.content: In 1863, Jules Verne did something he would almost never do again. He looked not toward an undiscovered island, the bottom of the sea, the interior of the Earth or the far side of the Moon, but directly into the future. He imagined Paris almost a century ahead, in the year 1960, and asked what sort of civilization the nineteenth century might become if its faith in science, machinery, commerce and efficiency were allowed to run to its logical conclusion. The result was Paris in the Twentieth Century, a book so unlike the Verne we came to know that his publisher, Pierre-Jules Hetzel, refused to publish it. Hetzel thought the prophecy implausible and the tone too bleak. Verne put the manuscript away. It remained unpublished for 131 years, until it was recovered from a family safe and finally appeared in France in 1994. We commonly describe Verne as a great…

items.title: The oldest ice disappears and the Stone Age emerges from it
items.author: dxs
items.content:
For exactly 20 years, archaeologists working with Secrets of the Ice have been recovering and preserving artefacts emerging from the ice in the mountains of Innlandet, eastern Norway.

Until now, most of the objects have been up to 2,000 years old. Many date from the Viking Age.

But the ancient ice is now beginning to melt.

And within this oldest ice lie the oldest finds: large quantities of arrow shafts and arrowheads from the Bronze Age and the Stone Age.

One of the oldest finds from this year's first field expedition is an arrow with an arrowhead and shaft made of slate.

By comparing it with previously discovered arrows, archaeologists estimate that it is between 5,000 and 6,000 years old.

The preservation conditions in the ice have meant that organic material, such as wood, leather, and textiles, have also survived.

“This year, we found 48 prehistoric arrows. That's a lot,” Espen Finstad, who leads Secrets of the Ice, tells Science Norway.

He explains that, with these latest discoveries, more than 100 arrowheads and arrow shafts have now been recovered from a single ice patch over the years.

The oldest arrowheads are made from slate, freshwater mussel shells, and bone. More recent arrowheads are made from iron and are 'only' between 1,000 and 1,500 years old.

But this year’s fieldwork carries an added sense of gravity.

Finstad explains that the work of recovering archaeological artefacts from the ice has always carried a certain duality.

“It’s fun going around looking for things. It’s exciting, and finding something is just really cool," he says.

Yet behind the excitement lies the reality of climate change. Finstad points to the recent landslide in Nepal and the glacier collapse in Jotunheimen.

“We have always acknowledged this contradiction and the reality behind our work. But this is the first time it has truly affected us on an emotional level,” Finstad says, adding:

“This year, there was a much deeper sense of seriousness and sadness. Only patches of ice remain where we once had large ice patches. It's brutal. And this year, that reality struck us more forcefully than ever before."

Finstad and his colleagues estimate that most of the ice patches containing archaeological artefacts will have disappeared within the next 20 years.

“There has been ice here for 6,000–7,000 years. Nature has been warning us and sending signals for many years. But now it's giving up. Now it is simply going to melt,” says the glacial archaeologist.

'For thousands of years, ancient ice has safely preserved unique objects from the past. Now that ice is disappearing,' the archaeologists write in a press release about the finds. 'We have been at the edge of the ice. We have seen it happening. And we are witnesses to a rapidly changing archaeological landscape.'

Finstad and his colleagues are planning more fieldwork in the coming weeks, weather permitting.

So far, they have secured finds in the Kvittingskjølen mountain area of Jotunheimen, specifically at Langfonne, Storefonne, and Hanklefonne.

Several of the finds are already on display at the Norwegian Mountain Centre in Lom, just a few days after they were discovered.

items.title: Infinite Mac: BeOS
items.author: ecliptik
items.content:
You can now run many BeOS versions in the browser at Infinite Mac, my site where you can experience the Macintosh Cinematic Universe from 1984 to 2005. The installs are full peers to their Mac cousins: you can boot them instantly (large disks are streamed in), play around with pre-installed software from Infinite HD, insert CD-ROMs from the Internet Archive, and save your work on the “Saved HD” drive.

BeOS was a multimedia-focused, multi-tasking and multi-threaded OS that was eventually ported to the Power Macintoshes of the mid-90s. It impressed many in the Mac community, including Apple itself, who considered acquiring Be, the company that had created it. If you’ve been following the saga of Apple’s search for a next-generation operating system, this lets you see what the road not taken was like.

After the last somewhat involved (though still satisfying) project on Infinite Mac, I was looking for a quicker win. BeOS had been on my radar for a while, and (unlike A/UX) I had a personal connection to it: I remember spotting a BeBox in Akihabara, making my Mac cosplay as it with BeView, and eventually dual-booting BeOS on my Power Macintosh 8500. DingusPPC, an emulator I had already integrated, was making good progress on running BeOS, so it seemed like adding it to the site would be mostly a matter of preparing some additional disk images.

Initially it appeared to be as straightforward as I had hoped; I added a Power Macintosh 7300 configuration (one of the Power Macs that was officially supported), found an install CD, made a disk image, and was up and running. But as I used it more and started to install additional versions, I began to find a lot of small bugs and edge cases:

  • The BeOS boot loader thought that all modifier keys were being held down due to a bug in the ADB emulation; this made it present the (ugly, PC BIOS-like) partition choice screen every time.
  • When changing the screen depth, there are two hardware components that need to be notified: the video controller and the digital-to-analog converter. DingusPPC had been accidentally relying on the order that Mac OS sent these notifications in; BeOS happened to make the opposite choice and would end up with a corrupted display.
  • Early versions of BeOS did video memory updates in little-endian mode; DingusPPC was missing support for that hardware capability.
  • Later versions of BeOS could mount HFS partitions, but they were having trouble with the volumes that I generated via the Python library. It turned out that BeOS was (correctly) stricter than Mac OS about how some data structures should be populated.

SheepShaver, a Power Macintosh emulator that is still around today (and that Infinite Mac also embeds), originated on BeOS. Mostly for the fun of another layer of inception/emulation, I wanted to make sure that it worked too. As it turned out, it also required a compatibility fix – it relied on an edge case of how the ROM is mapped to physical memory addresses that DingusPPC did not accurately model.

There is a pattern to most of these bug fixes: DingusPPC (and Infinite Mac) have been mostly focused on running Mac OS, and thus accidentally became dependent on its quirks or implementation choices. Adding an independently developed operating system to the mix exercised new paths, and ended up improving the accuracy of the emulated hardware. To be clear, DingusPPC was pretty close out of the box; kudos to itsmaintainers. I believe that, with this work, it’s the only emulator that can run PowerPC versions of BeOS. I’m also hopeful that this will help with bringing up alternate operating systems like MkLinux (which I also have memories of) and Rhapsody.

On the Infinite Mac side, there were obvious changes like a “BeOS” appearance for my custom controls and collecting software for the library. I also needed to overlay some dynamically generated content on the disk to get the OS to preselect a screen resolution that matches the browser window’s (similar to what was done for A/UX). An AI agent (still Codex for me) was once again helpful for this type of fiddly reverse-engineering task: it’s one thing to observe that the OS stores a file on disk with the screen size; it’s another to be able to reproduce all its nuances, especially as the format changed with later releases.

Developer Release 8.2, the initial BeOS version for Power Macs, had a time bomb that kept it from booting after April 1, 1997. This was not just to create a sense of urgency; it shipped with a licensed font renderer that Be could not distribute indefinitely. DR8.3 addressed this, but to make that notable first version bootable, I did end up relying on the custom date support to hardcode a working date when choosing that disk.

Though I did kick the tires of BeOS back when it was current, I don’t recall using it enough to form any opinions beyond “this is fast; I miss all my third-party software.” About This Particular Macintosh does have contemporary coverage, including Be’s first and second appearances at Macworld Expo Boston, and reviews of R3 and R4.5; they make for interesting reading. This video released by Be itself also has a walkthrough of what they considered its strengths.

Looking at it with 2026 eyes, I am still struck by its speed – it’s fast to boot and to use, especially when compared with its contemporary Mac OS releases that do so much less (e.g. live window dragging did not appear until Mac OS X). The POSIX subsystem and the Unix-like shell also feel modern (unlike A/UX’s) – I had no trouble using the terminal to poke around. There’s also plenty of innovation, though some of it (BFS with its attributes and live queries) is more interesting than the rest (replicants are a precursor to widgets, but I couldn’t think of a use for them).

It also feels like a developer-focused and under-construction system: many of the included apps are technology demos (though who doesn’t love a Utah teapot), while a contemporary Be homepage links directly to the developer release notes and discusses CodeWarrior releases and access to the bug tracker. The unfinished nature extends to third-party software too – I stumbled across some BeOS software on this Amiga magazine CD, and most of it had a “version 0.1” feel, either literally or figuratively. To be fair, I did find some more fleshed-out software, for example, Gobe Productive from the former ClarisWorks team. This and other software is on Infinite HD if you’d like to try it out (preferably in later OS versions).

The interface seemed novel at the time, though I wonder how it would have held up. The distinctive tabbed window titles look neat, but they have a reduced draggable area, so I’d have to think harder every time I wanted to move a window. And using a hand as the default cursor makes clicking feel less precise than a traditional arrow (just which of the pixels on the “finger” is the hotspot?). Other parts of the UI feel like a not-fully-coherent Windows/Mac hybrid, with a Deskbar that can emulate a Start menu, Alt key accelerators on menu items, but also spring-loaded folders and a spatial Tracker.

Speaking of the Tracker, I had not realized that Be had open-sourced it (and even incorporated changes from the open-source version). This was around the time that Be pivoted away to internet appliances – there’s no need to invest engineering resources in a file manager if all that’s exposed is one full-screen browser app. This interview with the Tracker developer has more of the backstory.

NeXTStep, by comparison, feels more mature. It had gone through some similar churn (proprietary hardware to off-the-shelf PCs, company strategy shifts), but, perhaps because it had more time, it handled things a bit more gracefully. For example, NeXT supported “fat” binaries that could run on 68K, Intel, PA-RISC and other architectures. On BeOS they had to be separate executables, making the user choose which to run and complicating distribution (this made it harder for me to find software to include in Infinite HD). Worse yet, you also had to have parallel disk partitions on CD-ROMs: BFS used the host endianness, so disks written by a PowerPC install could not be read by an Intel one, or vice versa. But my pro-NeXT bias may be due to knowing which OS Apple ended up picking.

It’s only been a short while since the last update, but I did squeeze in a couple of quality-of-life improvements. You can now take screenshots and record videos (with sound) of the emulated machine’s screen. This gives you a high-fidelity way to capture image content, since it’s a direct dump of what would have been shown on the screen.

I also expanded the collection of operating system CD-ROMs with items like the Rhapsody and Mac OS X developer previews. While they’re aspirational for now (DingusPPC can’t run them yet), they do satisfy my completionist tendencies. These CDs are mirrored to and served from my own Cloudflare R2 bucket – the Internet Archive is an incredible resource (you can donate to them), but streaming from it has been increasingly flaky. I don’t want to add to the problem, and thanks to my sponsors, I can afford to serve a few gigabytes.

As for what’s next, with this alternate Mac timeline covered, it may be time to explore a prequel.

items.title: AI, Lean, and the Future of Formal Verification, with Lean Creator Leo de Moura
items.author: datascientist
items.content:
Leo de Moura on Formal Proofs, AI Agents, and the End of “Trust Me” Code.

Ben Lorica speaks with , creator of , VP and Distinguished Scientist at , and Chief Architect of the Lean Focused Research Organization, about how AI is making formal verification more accessible and potentially transforming software engineering. They discuss the growing importance of specifications and machine-checked proofs, what it means to trust AI-generated code and autonomous agents, and the vision of a verified software stack. The conversation also explores how AI and formal verification are reshaping mathematics, what this means for the skills and careers of engineers and researchers, and where similar breakthroughs might emerge next.

Interview highlights – key sections from the video version:

Support our work by subscribing to our newsletter📩

Below is a polished and edited transcript.

All right. So today we have a treat. We have Leo de Moura, VP and Distinguished Scientist in the Automated Reasoning Group at AWS. More importantly, he is the creator of Lean, which can be found at lean-lang.org. Lean is both a programming language and a theorem prover, and he is also the Chief Architect of the Lean Focused Research Organization. So, with that long-winded introduction, Leo, welcome to the podcast.

Thank you, thank you. Very excited to be here.

All right. So, I guess the overarching thesis of this conversation is that we’re in an era where generation has become easy. Not necessarily cheap, as people who use Claude Code will attest, but easy. And so, one of the key challenges is verification. Lean is normally associated as the go-to tool. In fact, I think it’s going to be a tool that will increasingly be on the lips of many people in AI in the next year, around the topic of formal verification. So I guess let’s start here, Leo. Just the basics: for a listener who’s accustomed to code reviews, QA, and testing, what does formal verification mean?

Yeah, Lean is both a programming language and a proof assistant, right? You can write code, but also state properties the code should have. You can state open conjectures in math, and you can provide proofs of these claims, right? But the proof is not informal. The proof is written in the Lean language, and more importantly, it’s machine-checked.

Lean is a big piece of code, but to trust a result proved with Lean, you need to trust only the kernel, right? That’s where the proof is being checked. Like any other programming language, you have all the tooling: LSP server, IntelliSense, code generators, autocompletion. All these features are available in Lean, but they’re not important for the proof-checking step.

And we have more than one checker. In Lean, you can view proofs as data that can be manipulated, that can be transformed. You can export your proofs and check them with different checkers. Some of these checkers are verified now. We have two verified checkers. A third is coming soon.

But this ability to have machine-checkable proofs helps address a trust bottleneck, not just a trust bottleneck between humans, but also between humans and AI.

For example, suppose you want to synthesize a piece of code. You want to implement a piece of code that has specific properties. In the past, you would implement the software. Maybe you would add some testing infrastructure to make sure these properties hold. Property-based testing is very popular these days, right? And you would write the testing framework.

The testing framework is very useful for finding bugs, right? But it’s not useful for proving that there are no bugs.

You may even have a separate team conduct the testing.

Yes, yes. Now, with formal verification, you can start with the properties. You can, for example, write the properties down and ask the AI to implement a piece of code that satisfies these properties, and prove it to me. You’re going to implement the code and write a proof, a Lean proof, that will be machine-checked. And AI now is fully capable of doing that.

For example, a colleague and friend of mine, Kim Morrison, did an experiment where she ported zlib to Lean. This is a compression library. And now she has a property that says that if you compress data and then decompress it, you get the data back. There is no loss. The data was not corrupted. It’s an important property.

No matter the level of compression.

Exactly, exactly, exactly. Great, great. The theorem says exactly that. It’s one of the parameters of the theorem.

And so, Leo, for our listeners, she did this. She wrote this compression tool using Lean.

And then Lean served as kind of the formal verification tool. So if I’m a developer and I do the same thing, and I say I’m going to use Lean to formally verify my software, but I’m going to write it in Rust first, can Lean still help me?

Yes, yes, it can, in two different ways. The first way is using Aeneas. Aeneas is a tool that allows you to verify Rust code using Lean.

Aeneas is used, for example, by the SymCrypt team at Microsoft. SymCrypt is the cryptographic library at Microsoft. They use Aeneas plus Lean to verify the crypto library.

So you can start by using Aeneas. Another possibility is to ask your AI to build a model of your code in Lean. The AI will read your code, no matter—

No matter what language.

Yes, no matter what language. I mean, if someone had told me this last year, I would have said this is science fiction.

And this has a name, at least in mathematics. They call it autoformalization.

Right. So, in mathematics, for our listeners, you might have a math paper, and it’s a paper, so it’s composed of words, mathematical symbols, theorems, lemmas, and so on and so forth. And then autoformalization, which, as Leo points out, was not a thing—

As recently as maybe a year ago, it’s now a thing.
